name: Peak of a rise and fall
brief:
A new issue's price rose strictly every minute and then fell strictly every minute until the close. Either part may be empty. `path` lists the minute prices.

Write `peak_index(path)`, which returns the index of the highest price.

Example. For `path = [101, 104, 108, 107, 99]` the answer is 2.
constraints: $1 \le n \le 10^6$ prices, each a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$, rising strictly then falling strictly.
$O(\log n)$ time per call is the target. One hidden test makes 2,000 calls on a million prices, so `max` is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Compare the middle price with the next one. If the next is higher, the peak lies to the right; otherwise the middle could be the peak, so keep it.

examples.note: The price only fell, so the peak is the first minute.

tests.call: (lambda p: sum(peak_index(p) for _ in range(2000)))(list(range(500001)) + list(range(499999, -1, -1)))
(lambda p: sum(peak_index(p) for _ in range(2000)))(list(range(999990)) + [10**9] + list(range(8, -1, -1)))

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Whether the next price is higher tells which side of the peak the middle is on, so half the range goes each step.
Keep `hi = mid`, not `mid - 1`, when the price falls next: the middle itself may be the peak.

planted.slip: It scans for the first price that is higher than the next one, which is right but a million steps per call on 2,000 calls.
